article_title: Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation
citation: Reynolds, R., Walker, K., & Speight, C. (2010). Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.04.010
title: iGuides web-based museum trail system on PDAs at the Victoria and Albert Museum
description: The iGuides system, created by StreetAccess in 2004, links museum-created or external web pages into trails containing audio, text, video and images; users can input their own responses via photographs, voice recordings or text, creating personalised trails accessible on the web after the visit. Twenty trails were developed for HE design students at the V&A, hosted on the StreetAccess website and accessed via handheld PDAs over wireless networks installed in nine galleries.
requirements: Wireless network connectivity; handheld devices; the system relies on Internet connectivity to retrieve and store content.
constraints: When the network was not available the trails could not be used at all; image resolution was too low to study object details.
examples: Twenty trails were developed collaboratively with design tutors, students, designers and curators, including the 'thrill trail' and 'Break Into the V&A'.
key_sources: Reynolds, R., Walker, K., & Speight, C. (2010). Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.04.010

article_title: Pedagogic Effectiveness of Print, Interactive Multimedia, and Online Resources: A Case Study of IGNOU
citation: Jyotsna Dikshit, Suresh Garg, Santosh Panda. (2013). Pedagogic Effectiveness of Print, Interactive Multimedia, and Online Resources: A Case Study of IGNOU. International Journal of Instruction, 6(2). http://www.e-iji.net
title: Three-mode self-learning module on Computer Networks with integrated learning activities and the VirtualCampus.org virtual learning environment
description: The study's instructional artifact: the CIC Block 3 Unit 2 module on Computer Networks was restructured into a self-learning module of three small units equivalent to 15 hours of study and delivered in three modes — print with face-to-face support, an interactive multimedia CD, and a web-enabled version "with built – in discussion forum" posted on a specially designed website (VirtualCampus.org). Thirteen learning activities were integrated across the three modes, eight common to all, including pre-test, induction, study guide, self-assessment questions, discussion, chat, summary and post-test.
requirements: A personalised web server established for the online students
Two mentors at the server-end to facilitate chat and group discussions
Designated telelearning centres for the CD and online groups
constraints: The online module was tested for five days at two designated telelearning centres with 20 students, 10 at each centre
target_learners: Certificate in Computing students at IGNOU
target_learning_goals: computer networks content at certificate level
examples: The online daily schedule included going through the day's time-table, contents, web browsing, online quizzes, a 40-minute chat session, and discussion forum participation over the next full 24 hours
key_sources: Jyotsna Dikshit, Suresh Garg, Santosh Panda. (2013). Pedagogic Effectiveness of Print, Interactive Multimedia, and Online Resources: A Case Study of IGNOU. International Journal of Instruction, 6(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085398

article_title: Effects of Web-Based Interactive Modules on Engineering Students' Learning Motivations
citation: Bai, H., Aman, A., Xu, Y., Orlovskaya, N., & Zhou, M. (2016). Effects Of Web-Based Interactive Modules On Engineering Students' Learning Motivations. American Journal of Engineering Education, 7(2). https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJEE
title: IGLU: Interactive Web-Based Visualization Tools for Gluing Undergraduate Fuel Cell Systems Courses
description: IGLU is a web-based interactive visualization software package for undergraduate fuel cell courses, comprising five main modules: "introduction", "applications", "fuel cell system", "cell level", and "fuel cell science". Modules are highly interactive and interconnected, with animations, videos, audio narratives, and clickable links letting users jump between topics. It is intended as a supplementary classroom or outside-class tool, or the basis of a flipped classroom method.
requirements: Access via any web browser through a specific server or a website
constraints: Designed as a supplementary tool to enhance student learning rather than a standalone course
examples: Used as a 25-minute whole-class intervention in Data 1 and within a 50-minute class in Data 2
key_sources: Bai, H., Aman, A., Xu, Y., Orlovskaya, N., & Zhou, M. (2016). Effects Of Web-Based Interactive Modules On Engineering Students' Learning Motivations. American Journal of Engineering Education, 7(2). https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJEE

article_title: Learning curve in intestinal ultrasound: advancing from basic skills to advanced competencies-insights from the IUS IG-IBD Master program.
citation: Bezzio Cristina, Bertin Luisa, Saibeni Simone, Ribaldone Davide Giuseppe, Furfaro Federica, Maconi Giovanni, Terracciano Fulvia, Mazzotta Elena, Calabrese Emma, Castiglione Fabiana, Orlando Ambrogio, Privitera Giuseppe, Massironi Sara, Zorzi Francesca, Pirola Lorena, Danese Silvio, Rispo Antonio, Caprioli Flavio, Fraquelli Mirella, Pitoni Demis, Dal Buono Arianna, Testa Anna, Fantini Massimo Claudio, Armuzzi Alessandro, Allocca Mariangela. (2025). Learning curve in intestinal ultrasound: advancing from basic skills to advanced competencies–insights from the IUS IG-IBD Master program. Journal of Crohn's & Colitis. https://doi.org/10.1093/ecco-jcc/jjaf223
title: IG-IBD Master program three-phase competency-based IUS training curriculum
description: A standardized three-phase competency-based training curriculum implemented across eight Italian tertiary IBD centers. It comprises an intensive 8-h theoretical module covering "principles of IUS" including bowel wall anatomy, probe technical principles, vascular Doppler parameters, and case-based image interpretation; one week of supervised practical training with 30 supervised scans under expert sonographers; and an independent assessment phase of 99 examinations with blinded expert reassessment. Each trainee was paired with a single fixed expert throughout to ensure consistency in evaluation and feedback.
requirements: Expert sonographers with >2000 IUS examinations and a pre-study calibration session to standardize assessment criteria
Trainees paired with a single fixed expert throughout the study period
constraints: Designed for trainees with substantial general abdominal ultrasound experience (>200 examinations) but limited IUS exposure (<20 examinations)
target_learners: Gastroenterology trainees with prior abdominal ultrasound experience
target_learning_goals: Intestinal ultrasound competency for IBD assessment covering basic and advanced parameters
examples: Eight trainees each completed 129 total examinations: 30 supervised and 99 independent with blinded expert reassessment
key_sources: Bezzio Cristina, Bertin Luisa, Saibeni Simone, Ribaldone Davide Giuseppe, Furfaro Federica, Maconi Giovanni, Terracciano Fulvia, Mazzotta Elena, Calabrese Emma, Castiglione Fabiana, Orlando Ambrogio, Privitera Giuseppe, Massironi Sara, Zorzi Francesca, Pirola Lorena, Danese Silvio, Rispo Antonio, Caprioli Flavio, Fraquelli Mirella, Pitoni Demis, Dal Buono Arianna, Testa Anna, Fantini Massimo Claudio, Armuzzi Alessandro, Allocca Mariangela. article_title: Retrospective qualitative study evaluating the application of IG4 curriculum: an adaptable concept for holistic surgical education.
citation: Theodoulou Iakovos, Sideris Michail, Lawal Kola, Nicolaides Marios, Dedeilia Aikaterini, Emin Elif Iliria, Tsoulfas Georgios, Papalois Vassilios, Velmahos George, Papalois Apostolos. (2020). Retrospective qualitative study evaluating the application of IG4 curriculum: an adaptable concept for holistic surgical education. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-033181
title: Integrated Generation 4 (IG4): a three-dimensional surgical curriculum framework organised around skills, knowledge and module 'affinity'
description: IG4 is the newest version of the Cores Integrated for Research (Ci4R) curriculum, built on four cores (technical skills, non-technical skills, basic science, applied clinical science). Its defining feature is a third dimension: as the article states, IG4
requirements: Simulation infrastructure and faculty able to deliver modules across the four cores
Regional targets and speciality needs identified so module affinity can be mapped
constraints: Modules with higher affinity to one speciality are less applicable to other specialities
Delivered to date as a standalone course rather than embedded in medical school curricula
target_learners: Senior undergraduate medical students (year 3 and above)
target_learning_goals: Holistic surgical education spanning technical skills, non-technical skills, basic science and applied clinical science
examples: A theoretical application to orthopaedics and cardiothoracics (figure 1) shows shareable network nodes and speciality-specific module clusters across the four cores

article_title: Construction and preliminary evaluation of the inpatient glycemic control questionnaire (IGCQ): a survey tool assessing perceptions and knowledge of resident physicians.
citation: Horton William B., Law Sidney, Darji Monika, Conaway Mark R., Kubiak Nancy T., Kirby Jennifer L., Thigpen S. Calvin. (2019). Construction and preliminary evaluation of the inpatient glycemic control questionnaire (IGCQ): a survey tool assessing perceptions and knowledge of resident physicians. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1657-0
title: IGCQ: a 16-item preliminarily evaluated survey tool for resident physician perceptions and knowledge of inpatient glycemic control
description: The Inpatient Glycemic Control Questionnaire (IGCQ) is a survey tool constructed from four previously published but unvalidated surveys, assessing resident physicians' "comfort with managing IGC, knowledge of inpatient glycemic target values, and perceived barriers to successful IGC". It was evaluated with Rasch Partial Credit Model and classical test theory analyses across four US institutions, with 246 of 438 (56.2%) eligible residents completing it. The final 16-item version contains a comfort scale (Questions 1–6), a knowledge scale (Questions 7–10), and a barriers scale (Questions 11–16).
requirements: Administered with IRB approval and verbal consent at each institution; knowledge items retain five answer choices to preserve question complexity
constraints: Preliminary evaluation only: Rasch analysis covered one cohort of resident physicians, no DIF analyses were performed, and neither Rasch analysis of knowledge-based questions nor external validation were completed
target_learners: Internal medicine and medicine-pediatric resident and chief resident physicians
target_learning_goals: Assessing comfort, knowledge, and perceived barriers in inpatient glycemic control
examples: Administered in person and via Google Forms, QuestionPro, and SurveyMonkey at UMMC, Emory, UVA, and UL between February 2015 and May 2017
key_sources: Horton William B., Law Sidney, Darji Monika, Conaway Mark R., Kubiak Nancy T., Kirby Jennifer L., Thigpen S. Calvin. (2019). Construction and preliminary evaluation of the inpatient glycemic control questionnaire (IGCQ): a survey tool assessing perceptions and knowledge of resident physicians. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1657-0

citation: Silagadze, Z. K. (2007). Relativity without tears. https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.0929
title: The Ignatowsky one-postulate approach: deriving special relativity from the Relativity Principle alone
description: An alternative route to special relativity in which the Lorentz transformations follow from the Relativity Principle together with self-evident premises, without any light postulate. The article states that "the Relativity Principle alone along with some “self-evident” premises such as the homogeneity of space and time and the isotropy of space would suﬃce", a fact first discovered by von Ignatowsky in 1910 and largely neglected since. The author argues this approach is more appealing today because the luminiferous æther can no longer serve as the epistemological basis for the second postulate.
requirements: Acceptance of the Relativity Principle, space-time homogeneity and space isotropy as premises
constraints: The one-postulate derivations historically involved a higher level of mathematics, which the author suspects was considered an unnecessary complication making the approach unavailable for a general education physics course
target_learning_goals: understand the logical foundations of special relativity
derive Lorentz transformations without the light postulate
key_sources: Silagadze, Z. K. (2007). Relativity without tears. https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.0929
